wine.name: Prestige Brut
wine.grapes: Furmint and Chardonnay; earlier releases were mostly Furmint, and the estate's own recent sheet gives Chardonnay the larger part.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards on the slopes of Somló, a lone extinct volcano whose old lava flows left basalt over the hill.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method, the second fermentation taking place in the bottle, in the sparkling wine cellar the estate completed in 2011, with a cellar master from Champagne advising from the start. The wine rests on its lees for at least two years before disgorging, three years and more by the estate's recent sheet, and is finished Brut.
wine.glass: Lemon peel and pear with brioche from the long time on the lees, a fine, persistent mousse and a taut, salty finish of grapefruit pith carried by the high acidity of the hill.
wine.ageing: Ready on release and made to be drunk within a few years of disgorging, though a bottle kept a while longer gains toast and depth.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; never decanted; a tulip or white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: Hungarian for sparkling wine, the word on the back label.
Dry: only a little sugar is added in the dosage after disgorging.
The protected wine district of the hill, written Nagy-Somlói on a label.

records.table: Kreinbacher is the Somló estate that set out in 2002 to make bottle fermented sparkling wine on a volcanic hill known for its still white wines. Its Prestige Brut blends Furmint with Chardonnay and rests years on its lees; pour it cold as an aperitif.
records.story: Somló was known for still white wine, lean and smoky Juhfark and Furmint from the basalt of a lone extinct volcano, and by the estate's own account no house on the hill had made sparkling wine fermented in the bottle. In 2002 its founder, whose family name the house carries, bought his first vineyards on Somló with that plan in mind. The plan needed a cellar built for it, and in 2011 the estate completed its headquarters, winery and sparkling wine cellar, buildings shaped to echo the lava flows and basalt of the hill. A cellar master from Champagne has advised on the sparkling wines from the start, and the sparkling wines made there were released from 2014. Furmint, long grown on the hill, gave the wines their Hungarian accent, with Chardonnay beside it, while the estate kept making still Juhfark from the same slopes. Magyar Bor, the national wine body, has set Kreinbacher in the line of the sparkling wine houses Hungary built in the nineteenth century. For a sommelier, Prestige Brut is the bottle that shows Somló's acidity in a new form: proof that a hill famous for slow, smoky still whites can also make a long aged sparkling wine.

wine.name: Aranyhegy Juhfark
wine.grapes: Juhfark alone, the hill's own white grape, named for its long, tight bunch shaped like a sheep's tail.
wine.sites: Aranyhegy, the golden hill, one of the house's four named vineyards on Somló beside Grófi, Ilona and Apátsági, on the volcanic soils of the hill.
wine.making: The grapes are picked at low yields from Aranyhegy alone. By the sheet published for the 2022 vintage they were given a short maceration, pressed gently and fermented in oak barrels, then kept six months in barrel on their lees, which were stirred throughout.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon peel and quince over a smoky, flinty note from the volcanic soil, with restrained fruit, firm, tangy acidity and a long saline finish; honey and nuttiness come with years in bottle.
wine.ageing: Taut and closed when young; like all Juhfark it needs several years in bottle to round its acidity and show its honeyed depth, and it keeps well beyond that.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Sheep's tail: the grape is named for the long, cylindrical shape of its bunch.

records.table: Tornai is the Somló family house that traces its start to 1946, and its Aranyhegy Juhfark is the hill's own grape from one named vineyard, fermented in oak. It is smoky, saline and high in acid, so give it years and a cool glass.
records.story: Somló is a lone extinct volcano in the flat country north of Lake Balaton, and its wines were long prized in the Habsburg lands; a claim often repeated says Empress Maria Theresa (1717 to 1780) favoured them, and folk legend made Juhfark the wine of the wedding night, said to bring a son and heir. Tornai traces its start to 1946, when its founder planted a small plot on the hill. By the family's account it soon lost its land, as Hungary's farms were collectivised under communism, and private winemaking on the hill had to wait for the change of regime in 1990. After it the family gathered vineyards across the southern slopes, among them Aranyhegy, Grófi, Ilona and Apátsági, and Magyar Bor, the national wine body, counts Tornai among the larger houses making Juhfark. In 2021 the estate marked seventy five years, and it keeps a museum of the hill's history and its own beside the cellar. The house makes Juhfark at several levels, from a fresh Somlói bottling to wines of a single named vineyard. For a sommelier, the Aranyhegy Juhfark is the sheep's tail grape shown by one site, the way Somló's growers have long named their slopes.

wine.name: Juhfark
wine.grapes: Juhfark alone, the hill's own white grape of the long, sheep's tail bunch.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the south-eastern side of Somló, around the Apátság vineyard, on the volcanic soils of the hill.
wine.making: Pressed after six to twelve hours on the skins and fermented with wild yeast in old wood, then aged in large casks of oak and acacia for about a year, in the cellar's habit of one to three years before bottling. Some bottlings carry the name of the cask that raised them.
wine.glass: Quince, baked apple and lemon peel over smoke, wet stone and salt, with a broad, textured middle from the skin contact, high acidity and a long, slightly bitter almond finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and reserved for its first years, it is made to age: a good bottle develops over ten years and more, turning honeyed and nutty.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Kolonics is a small family cellar on the slope of Somló that works in the old way, with skin contact, wild yeast and long ageing in large oak and acacia casks. Its Juhfark is smoky, salty and slow to open, so pour it cool and give it air.
records.story: Kolonics is a family winery on the south-eastern slope of Somló whose history, by its own account, reaches back several generations. The first cellar came into the family in the late nineteenth century, when a great grandfather, a postmaster by trade, bought it, and much later the parents of the present winemaker gave it to him as a graduation gift. The family's own first wines followed in 2000, and the house counts 2001 as the year it took its shape. The winemaker is the fourth generation at the head of the family's estate and learnt its methods from his father and grandfather: grapes left a few hours on their skins, fermentation with wild yeast, and long rest in large old casks of oak and acacia before bottling. Some wines take their names from figures of Hungarian legend, among them the Juhfark bottlings called after their casks. In 2017 the house was among the category winners chosen for the Wine of the Hungarian Parliament. The family grows the hill's whites alone: Juhfark, Furmint, Hárslevelű and Olaszrizling among them. For a sommelier, Kolonics's Juhfark is the old Somló style, broad, smoky and saline, made to wait.

traps: A Kolonics Juhfark named for a cask, such as Töhötöm or Álmos, is Juhfark all the same: the name is the cask's, not a grape or a place.
Acacia here is the wood of the casks, a Hungarian tradition, not a flower note promised in the glass.

Founded is empty: the house dates its cellar to a great grandfather of the late nineteenth century and its own wines to 2000, with 2001 its milestone, and neither is a founding year.
The skin contact, wild yeast and oak and acacia casks rest on Decanter's 2019 note, the importer profiles and the Parliament page; the ageing of one to three years is the house's own.

The plan's why calls the ageing long; the sources read give about a year in cask for the 2019 Juhfark and one to three years in the cellar for the house, so the record says about a year and often longer.

wine.name: Somlói Juhfark
wine.grapes: Juhfark alone, the hill's own white grape, named for its bunch shaped like a sheep's tail.
wine.sites: The house's small holding on the southern side of Somló, in the Aranyhegy and Szent Márton vineyards, on the basalt and volcanic soils of the hill.
wine.making: Fermented with its own wild yeast and aged for about ten months in used oak casks of a thousand litres, then rested further in stainless steel. In the cellar's long habit the wines stay three to four years at the house before they are released.
wine.glass: Quince, ripe pear and lemon peel over smoke, flint and salt, with a firm, tangy acidity, a broad texture from the long rest and a long, savoury finish that turns honeyed and nutty with age.
wine.ageing: Released already a few years old, it is firm even then and opens further over many years in bottle, as the hill's Juhfark is known to do.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour to let it open; a white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Fekete is the small Somló cellar of an old winegrower known on the hill as its grand old man, and its Somlói Juhfark keeps his slow way: wild yeast, large used casks and years at the house before release. Pour it cool and give it time.
records.story: Fekete began, by the cellar's own account, in the early 1980s, when its founder, a winegrower who would become known on Somló as the hill's grand old man, set out on a small holding on the southern side of the hill and slowly enlarged it. He made white wine alone, from the hill's old grapes, Juhfark and Hárslevelű above all, with Furmint and Olaszrizling beside them, and he kept to the slow ways of the old cellars: fermentation with the wine's own yeast, large used casks and years of rest at the house before a wine was sold. In time his wines were among the Somló bottles that foreign writers and buyers sought out, a Juhfark of the 2008 vintage among those a British writer noted, and his Juhfark and Hárslevelű became the wines the house was known by. In 2014 the founder retired and passed the cellar to new owners, a small group of partners who bought it from him and set out to keep his methods and his style. The house has kept to releasing its wines only after three or four years in the cellar. For a sommelier, Fekete's Somlói Juhfark is the hill's grape as one of its older growers made it: patient, smoky and saline.

wine.name: Nagy-Somlói Juhfark
wine.grapes: Juhfark alone, the hill's own white grape, named for its bunch shaped like a sheep's tail.
wine.sites: The old abbey vineyard around the cellar on the south-eastern slope of Somló, put back together from many small parcels after 2001, facing the morning sun.
wine.making: Fermented with wild yeast in Hungarian oak casks and aged in the same wood, with nothing added in the cellar but the sulphur the wine needs; the vineyard has been farmed organically since 2017, by the cellar's own account.
wine.glass: Lemon peel, green pear and quince over smoke, wet stone and sea salt, lean and taut, with a firm line of acidity and a long, slightly bitter finish of almond skin.
wine.ageing: Tight and austere when young, it needs a few years to round its acidity and keeps well for a decade, gaining honey and nuttiness.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Of the abbey: the cellar and its vineyard once belonged to a Benedictine abbey.
Cellar: the Hungarian word for a winery's cellar and its house.

records.table: Somlói Apátsági Pince is the old abbey cellar of Somló, revived in 2001 on the vineyard the Benedictines of Pannonhalma once held. Its Nagy-Somlói Juhfark is wild fermented in Hungarian oak, lean, smoky and saline; pour it cool and give it time.
records.story: For centuries the church held vineyards on Somló, and several abbeys kept cellars on the hill, Zirc among them. By the cellar's own account, the vineyard that gives it its name, once known as the Viennese vineyard, passed early in the twentieth century to the Benedictine Archabbey of Pannonhalma, which worked it through its own vintner, a man of the Fazekas family, and its sale is recorded in 1911. In 1948, when the communist state nationalised the lands of the religious orders, the abbey's vineyard was broken up into small parcels, and the cellar with the little plot below it went to the vintner's family. In 2001 a group of partners bought the cellar building from that family and set about putting the old abbey vineyard back together from more than twenty parcels, replanting it with the hill's own white grapes. They named the house for the abbey, kept the old cellar, and work with wild yeast and Hungarian oak, and in 2017 they turned the vineyard to organic farming. For a sommelier, the abbey cellar's Juhfark is a reminder that the church shaped Somló's vineyards for centuries, and that a vineyard scattered under communism could be made whole again.

report: The tie to Pannonhalma is confirmed by the cellar's own history and a presentation of its own; the year of the archabbey's purchase is not clear from the search summaries (1901 or 1911, with a sale of 1911 for 53,800 korona), so the story says early in the twentieth century and names 1911 only as a recorded sale; a refuter should read the cellar's history page itself.
The founding partner of 2001 is living and is not named; neither is the vintner's grandson, who by the cellar's account still works in it.
The plan's doubt is answered: the house's Juhfark is the wine every trade page read shows first, and its own history ties it to Pannonhalma, so no swap is proposed.
Founded is 2001, the year the present house bought the cellar and began, as Magyar Bor's and the cellar's own pages give it; the cellar itself is older and its building date was not found.
The making is the cellar's own general account (Hungarian oak, wild yeast, sulphur alone, organic since 2017); no sheet for the Juhfark alone was found, so no time in cask is given.
The south-eastern aspect rests on the importer's note and Kolonics's address in the same Apátság vineyard.
